title: You cannot see the seer
hook: a practical man demands to be shown the self the way you'd point at a cow, and hears why it can never be pointed to
carry: the self is the seer, never the seen
tomorrow: the next man asks the same question, word for word. same answer?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhujyu's question from a spirit, and the razor-thin gap at the edge of everything; the wind carried the Parikshitas through. Your line was your breath is the world's breath.

A man starving in a famine eats leftover beans from an elephant driver to stay alive. Then the driver offers him water, and he turns it down: water, he says, I can find anywhere. That's Ushasti Chakrayana, in the Chandogya we read last month. Some readers take him to be today's challenger, Ushasta Chakrayana. Whoever he is, he's practical. He doesn't want theory. He wants to be shown. Point to it, he says, the way you'd point to a cow.
screen: `A MAN WHO SURVIVED ON LEFTOVER BEANS.` → `NO THEORY.` → `POINT TO IT.`

segments.voice: Yajnavalkya, he says, explain to me the Brahman that is right here, direct, not secondhand: the self that is within everything. That is your self, Yajnavalkya answers, within everything. Which one? The one that breathes in with your in-breath and out with your out-breath. That is your self, within all. Ushasta isn't having it. You've explained it the way someone says, that's a cow, that's a horse. I asked for the direct one. And here Yajnavalkya gives the answer this day is named for: na drishter drashtaram pashyeh. You cannot see the seer of seeing. You cannot hear the hearer of hearing. You cannot think the thinker of thinking. You cannot know the knower of knowing. That is your self, within all. Everything else is sorrow. And Ushasta falls silent. This is the atman, the self, as the Upanishads teach it. Everything you can point to is something seen. The self isn't something seen. It's what's doing the seeing. Your eye sees the whole room and never once sees itself. For Yajnavalkya, that doesn't make the self far away. It makes it nearer than anything you could point to. And it changes an ordinary day. We look at faces, screens, our own reflection, and quietly ask which of them is me. The Upanishad's answer: none of them. You're the one looking.
screen: `SHOW ME THE SELF WITHIN ALL.` · `NOT LIKE POINTING AT A COW.` · `YOU CANNOT SEE THE SEER OF SEEING.` · `ATMAN: THE ONE LOOKING.` · then, large: `THE SEER, NEVER THE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Hindu teachers call this self-inquiry. With your eyes open and soft, notice what you see, then gently try to turn around and find the one who's seeing; you won't find it as a thing. Close your eyes and do the same with sounds: hear, and then look for the hearer. Don't strain; rest in not finding it, and in the seeing still going on.
Ushasta. The man who wanted the self pointed out like a cow, and heard about the drashta, the seer, who can never be seen, because it is the one looking.
Hold on to it: the self is the seer, never the seen. Tomorrow, the same question asked again, word for word. Day three hundred seventy-five, done.

howItsDone: Teachers of Advaita Vedanta use this passage in self-inquiry, inviting students to turn attention back toward the one who sees; commentators of several Vedanta schools discuss the line about the seer of seeing.

fork.reveal: you cannot see the seer of seeing. the self isn't one more thing to point at; it's the one pointing. Ushasta falls silent.

original.note: Sanskrit draṣṭṛ (nominative draṣṭā): the seer, from dṛś, to see.

trapdoor: what you thought: Yajnavalkya dodged the question.
what it means: the self can't be shown, because it isn't something seen. it's the seeing itself.
what a scholar hears: na dṛṣṭer draṣṭāraṃ paśyeḥ (3.4.2). the Chandogya's Ushasti Chakrayana (1.10–11) is identified by some readers with this Ushasta.

notes: Ushasta (BU) and Ushasti (CU) Chakrayana: often identified, but not certain; the script says 'scholars often take him to be'. Confirm.

Chandogya 1.10: Ushasti eats kulmasha (beans/grain) left by an elephant driver (ibhya) and refuses the water as leftover. Confirm details ('last month' refers to the Chandogya block, days 332–359, though day 334 or nearby may not have told this story).
'Everything else is sorrow' renders ato 'nyad ārtam; confirm.
Sanskrit transliterated without diacritics: na dṛṣṭer draṣṭāraṃ paśyeḥ.
